subject: Climate & Environment
title: Overfishing and Collapse
description: A quick win: understand Overfishing and Collapse.

hook.text: 90% of the world's fish stocks are fully exploited or overfished. The ocean isn't limitless.

buildup.text: Industrial trawlers scrape the sea floor, catching everything and destroying habitats.

discovery.text: When a fish population crashes, the entire ecosystem reshuffles — often for the worse.

twist.text: The Atlantic cod fishery in Canada collapsed in 1992 after decades of overfishing. It still hasn't recovered.

climax.text: Three billion people depend on fish as their primary protein source.

punchline.text: We fish as if the ocean has no bottom. It does.

quiz.question: What percentage of global fish stocks are fully exploited or overfished?

details.summary: Over a third of global fish stocks are overfished, and another 60 percent are fished at their maximum sustainable limit. Industrial fleets using sonar and massive nets have depleted populations faster than they can reproduce, causing stock collapses that devastate marine ecosystems.
details.whyItMatters: Fish provide essential protein for over three billion people. Overfishing not only threatens food security but destroys marine ecosystems that regulate ocean health.
takeaways: Over a third of fish stocks are overfished globally
Industrial technology has dramatically increased catch capacity
Stock collapses can take decades to recover from, if at all

faq.question: What is the most famous example of a fishery collapse?
faq.answer: The collapse of Atlantic cod off Newfoundland in 1992 is the best known. Decades of industrial overfishing reduced the population by 99 percent. Canada imposed a moratorium, but more than 30 years later the stock has still not fully recovered.

faq.question: How does overfishing affect marine ecosystems?
faq.answer: Removing top predators triggers trophic cascades that restructure entire food webs. Overfishing also damages seabed habitats through bottom trawling, reduces genetic diversity in fish populations, and undermines ecosystem resilience.
